Inspect the Arithmetic: Sole Proprietor vs Corporation Calculator

Version 1.1
Last verified: May 2026

This page explains how the Sole Proprietor vs Corporation Calculator compares personal / RRSP investing with retained corporate investing. The goal is to show how much after-tax capital is available to invest after personal spending needs are met.

Purpose

Both paths use the same gross business income and the same target after-tax lifestyle spending. The calculator asks how much remains available as first-year invested capital under each structure—not which structure has the lowest headline tax in isolation.

Inputs

Input Meaning
Gross business income Active business or professional income before tax. The same gross is compared in both columns.
Province / territory & tax year Drives personal tax integration and provincial corporate rate components. Data files match the site’s Canada Personal Income Tax Calculator and CCPC Income Tax Calculator.
After-tax spending need Annual lifestyle spending after personal income taxes. Both structures are solved around this constraint.
RRSP room & contribution Maximum deductible contribution is capped by room, income, and the annual dollar limit in the federal tax file. Auto mode uses the minimum of those.
Refund reinvestment When on, the estimated RRSP refund is counted as non-registered capital. It is not also included in “surplus” cash (the ledger avoids double counting).
Corporate tax rate Defaults to statutory federal + provincial small-business combined rates from JSON; income above the small-business limit blends to general federal + provincial rates. Optional flat override replaces the split model.
Withdrawal type Simple mode pays non-eligible dividends from after-tax corporate cash and solves the minimal gross dividend such that net take-home meets spending. Salary and blend modes use the same personal tax engine.
Expected return & projection years Optional compound projection: futureValue = investedCapital × (1 + annualReturn)years. Corporate side may apply an optional passive drag percentage to the return.

Personal / sole proprietor path

  1. Taxable income after RRSP: taxableIncome = grossIncome − rrspContribution (plus dividend gross-ups only if applicable — here business income is modeled as self-employment).
  2. Personal tax with RRSP: federal + provincial net tax from the shared engine.
  3. Personal tax without RRSP: same inputs with rrspDeduction = 0.
  4. RRSP refund (incremental): rrspRefund = taxWithoutRRSP − taxWithRRSP on income tax (not CPP/EI timing).
  5. Wallet after RRSP cash contribution: takeHomeAfterPayroll − rrspContribution, where take-home uses taxes computed with the RRSP deduction.
  6. Non-registered surplus invested: max(0, wallet after RRSP − spending need), optional toggle.
  7. Total invested capital:
    personalInvestedCapital = rrspContribution + reinvestedRefund + nonRegisteredSurplusInvested

Corporate path

  1. Corporate tax on active income: blended small-business pool then general pool, unless a flat effective override is supplied.
  2. After-tax corporate income (pre-distribution): grossCorporateIncome − corporateTax for dividend-from-retained-earnings mode; salary mode deducts salary before taxing corporate income.
  3. Required withdrawal: smallest salary and/or non-eligible dividends such that estimated personal net cash ≥ spending need (binary search), respecting that dividends cannot exceed corporate cash after salary and corporate tax (blend mode uses a bounded grid search).
  4. Retained corporate capital:
    corporateRetainedCapital = afterTaxCorporateCash − corporateCashPaidOutForWithdrawals

Comparison

difference = corporateRetainedCapital − personalInvestedCapital

Percentage advantage vs the losing structure:
percentageAdvantage = |difference| / losingStructureCapital when the loser’s capital base is positive.

Projection

futureValue = investedCapital × (1 + annualReturn)years on each side independently. Corporate projection may reduce the return by an optional passive tax drag field.

This projection is pre–final-withdrawal-tax unless you layer in your own assumptions about RRSP withdrawals and taxable distributions later.

Limitations

  • Tax rates and thresholds change; data files are versioned by year.
  • Dividend integration is implemented via the site’s dividend gross-up / credit tables—reasonable for education, not a substitute for professional integration planning.
  • Passive investment income inside corporations has Part I / Part IV rules not modeled except via the optional drag field.
  • RRSP withdrawals are taxable later; corporate distributions are taxable later.
  • CPP on self-employment and other payroll nuances may differ from your notice of assessment.
  • Accounting, legal, and compliance costs are excluded unless you treat them implicitly by adjusting inputs.
